name: CaddyMate
summary: An assistive shopping trolley that guides older shoppers to each item and lifts their groceries so they don't have to bend.
highlights: Won Amazon's Runner-Up Prize with a team of 8, building an assistive shopping robot for older and mobility-impaired shoppers.
Modelled and 3D-printed every part of the frame except the screen arm in Autodesk Inventor, prototyping handles in PLA and TPU for grip and comfort.
Prototyped the hooks attaching the TurtleBot base to the frame, and laser-engraved the logo onto the acrylic walls.
Worked as assistant project manager, acting as the technical bridge between the frame, base and robotics teams.
In testing, 93% of users found it easy to use, and it reached its target in every end-to-end trial.

screenshot.alt: CaddyMate: a black trolley on an aluminium frame, with two handles and a touchscreen on an arm, on a pink-to-orange background.

gallery.caption: The finished prototype: the supportive frame, textured handles and touchscreen on its arm.
The raising base lifting a bottle up to hand height, controlled from the screen.
The scissor-lift base going up and down inside the frame.
An early build of the robotic base driving itself towards a goal in the test arena.
The map screen planning a route to the bagels in aisle 3.
Part of the team at the industry day, beside our poster.

name: Reverse CAPTCHA
summary: A CAPTCHA that lets AI agents in, keeps humans out, and works out what kind of visitor just arrived.
highlights: Built solo at the Edinburgh AI Hackathon. Classifies each visitor as a human, scraper, browser agent or vision agent from pointer paths, click offsets, key timings and browser signals.
Gives machine-like visitors a generated 1,900-word document and a 6-second question timed on the server, with a hidden instruction that separates agents reading the page's code from vision agents.
Routes agents on demo sites to a structured JSON lane with no visible CAPTCHA, with a live dashboard and Pytest suites for the rules, features and API.

screenshot.alt: Reverse CAPTCHA's gate: "Prove you're not human" above an "I am not a human" checkbox.

gallery.caption: A person ticks the box and is turned away: their mouse moved too much like a human's.
Machine-like visitors get a 1,900-word document and 6 seconds to answer a question about it.
A browser agent passes in about 3 seconds and is shown every reason for its verdict.
A mock flight site with no CAPTCHA, where the same checks quietly route agents to their own lane.
The live dashboard: a human-to-machine meter, recent attempts and traffic in each lane.

name: Blockr
summary: A privacy-first website blocker for Chrome that keeps all its data on your device.
highlights: Built and published a privacy-first extension on the Chrome Web Store, keeping all data local with no backend.
Blocked sites via Manifest V3's declarativeNetRequest API, with schedules, daily time limits and a password lock.
Wrote Vitest suites covering blocking rules, schedules, usage tracking and storage migrations.
Designed the UI in Figma, with light and dark themes audited to ensure they meet WCAG AA contrast.

screenshot.alt: Blockr's popup, with a pause blocking button and switches for blocking social media and short-form content.

name: WikiWatch
summary: Turns Wikipedia's live edit stream into newsroom-style headlines with a local LLM, then reads the mood of each one.
highlights: Built at Hack the Burgh 2025 in a team of 6.
Built the front-end, moving the interface to a Next.js and React app.
Built the live headline feed and the positive, neutral and negative mood stats.

screenshot.alt: WikiWatch's bubbles: live Wikipedia edits rewritten as headlines, coloured blue, gold or red by mood.

gallery.caption: A burst of edits: each bubble is a generated headline, sized by the edit and coloured by its mood, with the latest headlines on the left.
Hovering a bubble shows the edit behind it: the editor, its size, the wiki, the edit comment and the headline's mood.
Edinburgh Mode only keeps articles a few links away from Edinburgh's page on Wikipedia.

name: Zen
summary: A focus and productivity app for Android, designed in Figma first.
highlights: Designed the app in Figma from stakeholder feedback, then built it in Kotlin with a pomodoro timer, task reminders and streak stats, earning the Edinburgh Award (Digital Skills Specialist).
Set up GitHub Actions CI running lint, unit tests and Espresso UI tests on an emulator, with automated accessibility checks on every UI interaction.

screenshot.alt: Zen's logo: three green petals above the word Zen.

name: This website
summary: A retro pixel-art portfolio, built one small pull request at a time.
highlights: Draws every sprite from typed string grids as crisp SVGs, checked by tests.
Keeps experience, projects and skills in data files validated with Zod, so a typo fails CI.
Runs lint, type checks and unit tests on every pull request, and Playwright against each Vercel preview.
